narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average accepted student ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the bottom decile. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your first-year ranking worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. At the 6th decile, you matched the exact average of students who were admitted, giving the model some reassurance about your early academic ability.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and again pushed toward failure. At 26.5, it sits well below the 37.2 average of accepted students, indicating the model saw this as another meaningful risk for bar exam performance.

Taken together, the weak third-year performance and lower LSAT outweighed your solid first-year results, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening your academic record and retaking the LSAT. Improving both would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction and give you a much stronger application in the future.
